content: Oral lesions are also referred to as oral cavity lesions, oral cavity ulcers, oral cavity infections, mouth ulcers, and mouth lesions. In many instances, mouth sores are caused by the herpes simplex virus or idiopathic aphthous stomatitis. However, oral lesions may also signify a more serious underlying condition. To achieve an accurate diagnosis, a comprehensive review of the patient’s systemic health and a thorough skin examination are essential. The pathophysiology and differential diagnosis of oral cavity lesions have been extensively studied. For example, Jahanbani et al. (2009) evaluated oral mucosal lesions in 598 Iranian patients, highlighting the importance of clinical assessment in identifying these conditions. Similarly, Abidullah et al. (2016) conducted a study on white, non-scrapable oral mucosal surface lesions, emphasizing the need for clinico-pathologic correlation. Fordyce spots, a common benign finding, have been investigated in various studies. Lee et al. (2012) described the clinico-pathologic manifestations of Fordyce spots, while Olivier (2006) explored their prevalence in specific populations. Additionally, De Felice et al. (2005) examined the association between Fordyce granules and hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer syndrome. Geographic tongue, also known as benign migratory glossitis, is another enigmatic oral lesion. Assimakopoulos et al. (2002) and Picciani et al. (2016) provided insights into its clinical, histopathological, and genetic correlations, including its potential link to psoriasis. Black hairy tongue, a condition characterized by elongated filiform papillae, has been documented in various case studies. Kobayashi et al. (2010) described its dermoscopic features, while Gurvits and Tan (2014) reviewed its clinical presentation and management. Oral hairy leukoplakia, often associated with immunosuppression, has been extensively studied. Kreuter and Wieland (2011) identified it as a clinical indicator of immunosuppression, and Greenspan et al. (2016) provided a comprehensive review of its pathogenesis and clinical implications. White sponge nevus, a rare genetic condition, has been reported in case studies such as those by Aghbali et al. (2009) and Nichols et al. (1990). These studies highlight its characteristic clinical and histological features. Lichen planus, a chronic inflammatory condition, affects both cutaneous and mucosal surfaces. Gorouhi et al. (2014) and Gupta and Jawanda (2015) reviewed its clinical subtypes, risk factors, and management strategies. Oral candidiasis, commonly caused by Candida species, has been explored in studies like those by Williams and Lewis (2011) and Warrier and Sathasivasubramanian (2015). These studies emphasize the importance of accurate diagnosis and appropriate antifungal therapy. Histoplasmosis, a systemic fungal infection, can present with oral manifestations. Chatterjee et al. (2017) and Vidyanath et al. (2013) documented cases of disseminated histoplasmosis with oral involvement, underscoring the need for early recognition and treatment. Coccidioidomycosis, another systemic fungal infection, may also involve the oral cavity. Mendez et al. (2017) and Rodriguez and Konia (2005) reported cases of oral lesions as a manifestation of systemic disease. Pemphigus vulgaris, an autoimmune blistering disorder, frequently involves the oral mucosa. Arpita et al. (2015) and Kumar et al. (2016) described its clinical presentation and diagnostic approaches, including direct immunofluorescence studies. Mucous membrane pemphigoid, a chronic autoimmune condition, can present with desquamative gingivitis. Vijayan et al. (2016) and Trimarchi et al. (2009) highlighted its clinical features and management. Recurrent aphthous ulcers, a common condition, have been studied for their etiology and treatment. Altenburg et al. (2014) reviewed therapeutic options, while Bucciarelli et al. (2006) explored their association with systemic conditions like celiac disease. Erythema multiforme, a hypersensitivity reaction, can involve the oral mucosa. Scully and Bagan (2008) and Joseph et al. (2012) documented its clinical variants and potential triggers, including medications. Oral epithelial dysplasia, a precursor to oral cancer, has been extensively studied. Speight (2007) reviewed its progression to malignancy, emphasizing the importance of early detection and intervention. Rare oral tumors, such as rhabdomyomas, hemangiomas, and Kaposi’s sarcoma, have been reported in case studies. Zhang et al. (2012) and Dilsiz et al. (2009) provided insights into their clinical presentation and management. Congenital oral lesions, such as granular cell epulis and ectomesenchymal chondromyxoid tumors, have also been documented. Vered et al. (2009) and Angiero (2010) described their histological and immunohistochemical features. Cysts of the oral cavity, including lymphoepithelial cysts and thyroglossal duct cysts, have been reported in various studies. Sykaras et al. (2017) and Burkart et al. (2009) highlighted their clinical and radiological characteristics. This comprehensive review underscores the diverse etiologies and clinical presentations of oral lesions, emphasizing the importance of accurate diagnosis and tailored management strategies.
